name: Grizzly

archived.reason: Grafana Labs deprecated Grizzly in May 2025 in favour of a new CLI, grafanactl (itself since superseded by gcx). The last commit, marking it deprecated, landed on 1 July 2025; the repository has since moved to the grafana-cold-storage organisation and been archived, its docs site is gone, and Grafana’s docs say it is no longer enhanced or supported.

summary: Grafana Labs’ deprecated `grr` command line tool for keeping Grafana dashboards, alert rules and data sources as YAML, JSON or Jsonnet files and pushing them to Grafana.
intro: Grizzly describes observability resources as files in a Kubernetes-like format: an `apiVersion`, a `kind` (Dashboard, DashboardFolder, Datasource, AlertRuleGroup, contact points and notification policies, library elements, Prometheus rule groups or Grafana Cloud synthetic monitoring checks), `metadata` with a name and folder, and a `spec` holding the resource itself. You write these by hand in YAML or JSON, or generate them with Jsonnet, often with libraries such as Grafonnet. `grr diff` compares the files with what is live, `grr apply` uploads them through Grafana’s HTTP API, `grr pull` downloads existing resources (useful for copying dashboards between instances), and `grr watch` re-applies on every save. Contexts hold each instance’s URL and service account token.

Its last notable feature, `grr serve`, ran a local proxy in front of a real Grafana: dashboards were read from disk and rendered with Grafana’s UI and data sources without being published, and saving in the browser wrote the change back to the file. With `-w` it reloaded on file changes, including dashboards generated by Jsonnet or by TypeScript, Go or Python code. Grafana Labs deprecated Grizzly in May 2025 and has since archived it; its last release is 0.7.1 (January 2025), and Homebrew plans to disable the formula in February 2027.
strengths: Dashboards, alert rules and data sources kept in git and applied from CI, so a deploy updates monitoring along with the code
First-class Jsonnet: generate many similar dashboards and rules from shared libraries such as the monitoring mixins
`grr serve` let you edit and review file-based dashboards in a real Grafana without publishing them
No state file: it diffs local files against the live instance directly
limits: Archived and unsupported: no fixes, including security fixes, and its documentation site is offline
Built on older Grafana APIs that were not designed for tooling, which forced workarounds and is why Grafana Labs replaced it
Covers fewer resources than the Grafana Terraform provider, which also manages Grafana Cloud resources such as collectors and access
Pulled data sources come back without their secure passwords, which have to be filled in by hand

story: Malcolm Holmes, an engineer at Grafana Labs, made the first commit in March 2020. The early README called Grizzly “a utility for managing Jsonnet dashboards” through the Grafana REST API, built to work with monitoring mixins, packages of Jsonnet dashboards and alerts. Its status was “Alpha. This is a proof of concept.”

Over the next four years it grew from dashboards to folders, data sources, Prometheus and Grafana alert rules, contact points and Grafana Cloud synthetic monitoring checks, moved from Jsonnet-only conventions to Kubernetes-style resource files, and in 2024 added `grr serve` for editing file-based dashboards inside a live Grafana.

In May 2025 Grafana Labs announced that Grizzly would be phased out in favour of grafanactl. Its first CLI had been built on APIs that were not very tooling-friendly, and the newer Grafana APIs treat every resource the same way, so a fresh tool was simpler than a Grizzly 2.0. grafanactl dropped built-in Jsonnet, leaving that to jsonnet itself, and has in turn been replaced by gcx.

choices.choice: Jsonnet as the main way to write resources
choices.why: Dashboards are large JSON documents with much repetition. Jsonnet functions and libraries, as used in the monitoring mixins, generate them from a few lines.
An `apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata` and `spec` let one tool handle dashboards, alert rules and synthetic checks in the same files, independent of the language that produced them.

choices.choice: Talk to the live API, keep no state
choices.why: Diffing files against the running Grafana avoids a separate state file, at the cost of having to work around APIs that were not designed for tooling.
